slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Wet or dirty syringes, needles and tubes, a long-applied tourniquet and forceful transfer cause haemolysis.
Separate plasma or serum from the cells as soon as possible; close containers well to prevent evaporation and store only in plastic containers.
If the analysis cannot be done within 4 hours of drawing the blood, the specimen is frozen.
Do not test turbid, haemolysed or lipaemic serum/plasma, or serum with very high bilirubin.
The material is kept until all analyses are finished — the test can be repeated if needed.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood; in certain cases cerebrospinal, peritoneal or pleural fluid

What it is used for: LDH is mainly used to check for tissue damage. It may help diagnose or monitor diseases of the blood (including anemia), liver, lungs, kidneys, heart (including heart attack), pancreas, brain and spinal cord, and help monitor conditions that may worsen over time, such as muscular dystrophy and HIV.

It may also help diagnose certain severe infections, show how serious some cancers are (multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, melanoma) and check whether treatment for certain cancers is working.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: LDH (lactate, or lactic acid, dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that helps cells make energy and is found in almost all tissues, with the largest amounts in muscles, liver, kidneys and red blood cells. When disease or injury damages these tissues, the cells release LDH into the blood or other body fluids.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
cols: In general, higher-than-normal LDH usually means some type of tissue damage, usually from disease, infection or injury; more tests may be needed to diagnose the condition.

Lower-than-normal LDH is uncommon and usually not considered a health problem. Taking large amounts of vitamin C or vitamin E, or the rare genetic disorder lactate dehydrogenase deficiency, may cause low levels.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for an LDH blood test. For other fluids (cerebrospinal fluid by lumbar puncture, chest fluid by thoracentesis, abdominal fluid by paracentesis) the provider explains how to prepare.

Interferences: A high LDH does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: intense exercise and certain medicines, including aspirin, can raise it. LDH can also be high if many red blood cells broke open while the sample was collected and tested (hemolysis).

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Limitations: An LDH test alone cannot show what is damaging tissues or where the damage is, so it is usually done with other tests. The meaning of a result depends on why the test was done, the symptoms and other test results.
If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test, which measures five forms of LDH, may be ordered to help find the type and location of the damaged tissue and how serious the damage is.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to screen for or help diagnose liver and bone diseases and to help diagnose or monitor other conditions. Often done with a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) or liver function tests, or when there are symptoms of liver damage or a bone disorder (bone pain, joint inflammation, unusually shaped or enlarged bones, broken bones).
Physiology: ALP is an enzyme present in all body tissues, with higher amounts in the liver, bile ducts and bones. Each part of the body makes a different type of ALP.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: High ALP from the liver may be a sign of bile duct blockage, cirrhosis, hepatitis or mononucleosis (which can sometimes cause swelling in the liver).
If ALP is high and liver tests are normal, a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone is possible.

Low ALP is less common. Possible causes: zinc deficiency, protein deficiency, malnutrition, pernicious anemia, thyroid disease, Wilson disease and hypophosphatasia (a rare genetic disease affecting bones and teeth).

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: Moderately high ALP may occur with many conditions, including Hodgkin lymphoma, heart failure and certain infections; a high ALP may also occur without a condition that needs treatment.
Cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase is raised out of proportion to ALT and AST.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: A raised GGT supports a liver source. If bilirubin rises too, bile-duct obstruction is considered.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALP is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: Pregnancy can raise ALP, and children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing. Birth control pills and some medicines may lower ALP while others raise it, and a fatty meal before the test may cause a small increase.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Limitations: The ALP test alone cannot tell which tissue the ALP comes from, so other tests are usually needed. An ALP isoenzyme test can show its source (not available everywhere); if liver function tests are also high, the ALP is likely of liver origin.

Abnormal liver test results don't always mean a liver problem: high ALP, for example, can be a sign of bone disease as well as liver disease. The provider also considers symptoms, medical history, liver disease risk and medicines taken.
